title: United to block customers from using AI agents, citing cyber threats
content:
United to block customers from using AI agents, citing cyber threats
United Airlines will block AI agents from managing customers’ reservations and flight purchases, warning of significant cybersecurity and privacy risks, as well as potential legal violations.
Other large corporations have made similar announcements recently, including Bank of America, which cautioned users last week to never share user IDs and passwords with agents.
Many companies, particularly banks and airlines, have faced mounting difficulty as they try to separate human customers from their AI assistants. The firms warn that consumers’ credentials are at risk of leaking when they entrust agents with their logins and passwords.
“Sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles,” United said in a Wednesday press release.
Automated AI actions also could break Federal Aviation Administration and Department of Transportation rules, the release said, citing the fact that flight check-in requires “human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances like explosives.”
The airline is implementing the new access restrictions both within its own digital platforms and separately through aggregators and agencies.
“This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies,” the press release said.
But United and other corporate giants’ moves are not a long-term cure all, according to Raj Ananthanpillai, founder and CEO of identity verification company Trua.
“Blocking agents or forcing more data sharing just delays the inevitable,” he said via text, arguing for wider use of verified identity tokens.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

report.summary: United Airlines will block AI agents from booking and managing reservations, citing cybersecurity, privacy and regulatory risks, as companies struggle to distinguish humans from automated assistants.
report.background: The move comes as agentic AI tools increasingly act on consumers’ behalf online, including booking travel, managing accounts and completing purchases. Many of these agents rely on users sharing login credentials or screen-scraping, making it hard for companies to tell a legitimate customer from a bot. Banks and airlines have warned that credential sharing can expose sensitive data and enable unauthorized transactions. United also faces sector-specific rules: FAA and DOT requirements can demand human acknowledgment during check-in, such as confirming bags contain no banned substances. The airline says it will enforce restrictions through its own platforms and through aggregators and agencies, updating booking, ticketing and distribution policies. The dispute reflects a broader tension between convenience-driven AI automation and corporate security, liability and regulatory compliance.
key_points: United will block AI agents from managing reservations, flight purchases and MileagePlus actions. The restrictions apply both on United’s own digital platforms and through aggregators and agencies, with updates to booking, ticketing and distribution policies. United says the change is meant to reduce cybersecurity, privacy and legal exposure.

United warns that sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants can leak sensitive information and lead to unintended purchases, account changes or misuse of MileagePlus miles. The airline is trying to separate human customers from automated assistants that may log in using a customer’s credentials.

Regulatory compliance is a central concern. United says automated AI actions could violate FAA and Department of Transportation rules, noting that flight check-in requires human acknowledgment that bags do not contain banned substances such as explosives.

Other large companies are taking similar steps. Bank of America recently warned customers never to share user IDs and passwords with agents, illustrating how banks and airlines are struggling to manage AI assistants that act on behalf of consumers.

Experts say blocking agents is not a long-term fix. Trua CEO Raj Ananthanpillai argued that blocking agents or forcing more data sharing only delays the inevitable, and called for wider use of verified identity tokens to safely authenticate users and delegated agents.
report.impact: For the AI industry, United’s move signals that agentic AI cannot rely on credential sharing or browser automation alone. Developers building travel, finance or account-management agents will need delegated authorization, scoped permissions, audit logs, consent screens and human-in-the-loop checks for sensitive actions. Companies may increasingly wall off services or impose terms that classify agents as unauthorized bots, slowing agent interoperability. For regular users, the immediate effect is less convenience: assistants may fail at booking or check-in, and users may need to complete steps manually. Longer term, the conflict could push adoption of identity standards and verified-agent tokens that preserve automation while giving companies clearer liability, security and compliance controls.
report.tools: Readers tracking delegated agent access should watch OAuth 2.1/PKCE, OpenID Connect, FIDO2/passkeys, and emerging agent-authorization profiles. Open-source projects worth testing include Keycloak, Ory Hydra, OpenFGA for fine-grained permissions, and SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity. Commercial identity platforms such as Auth0 and Okta are also adding agent-focused controls. For developers building browser agents, pair Playwright or browser-use with explicit consent screens, scoped tokens, audit logs, and human-in-the-loop confirmation before purchases or check-in.
